title: Peripheral Nerves
subtitle: Localizing a mononeuropathy from its motor, sensory and reflex territory, and the site of compression

points.text: Complete sensory loss from a divided nerve occurs only in its autonomous zone, so that zone must be sought specifically.
points.quote: all modalities of cutaneous sensibility are lost only over the area exclusively supplied by that nerve (the autonomous zone)

points.text: With nerve lesions, light touch loss is wider than pinprick loss.
points.quote: In general, with peripheral nerve lesions, the area of light touch sensory loss is greater than the area of pinprick sensory loss.

points.text: Axons stay grouped by fascicle along the nerve, which is why partial lesions can mimic lesions at other sites.
points.quote: Evidence indicates that specific axons remain grouped together, particularly through their distal course, as they travel toward their destination

points.text: The median nerve forms in the axilla from the lateral cord (C6-C7) and medial cord (C8-T1).
points.quote: formed in the axilla by the joining of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus (spinal segments C6-C7) with the medial cord

points.text: The purely motor anterior interosseous branch supplies flexor pollicis longus, flexor digitorum profundus I and II, and pronator quadratus.
points.quote: the median nerve gives off the purely motor anterior interosseus nerve, which innervates the following muscles

points.text: The palmar cutaneous branch leaves above the wrist and supplies the thenar eminence skin, so it does not pass through the carpal tunnel.
points.quote: palmar cutaneous branch, which crosses the flexor retinaculum either subcutaneously or through the superficial ligament fibers to supply the skin over the thenar eminence

points.text: At the elbow the ulnar nerve runs through the cubital tunnel, whose roof is the aponeurosis between olecranon and medial epicondyle.
points.quote: The aponeurosis between the olecranon and medial epicondyle forms the roof of an osseofibrous canal (the cubital tunnel)

points.text: Its first muscular branches, just below the elbow, go to flexor carpi ulnaris and to the ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus.
points.quote: the nerve gives off its first two muscular branches, to the flexor carpi ulnaris and the flexor digitorum profundus III and IV, respectively.

points.text: The palmar cutaneous branch (hypothenar skin) arises in the distal forearm, before the wrist; a dorsal cutaneous branch follows.
points.quote: in the distal forearm, gives off the palmar cutaneous branch, which supplies the skin over the hypothenar eminence

points.text: At the wrist the deep motor branch passes between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate (Guyon canal).
points.quote: passes between the pisiform carpal bone medially and the hook of the hamate carpal bone laterally (ulnar tunnel or canal of Guyon)

points.text: The radial nerve arises from the posterior cord and carries C5-C8 fibers.
points.quote: derives from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus and comprises fibers from the spinal levels C5-C8

points.text: The triceps and anconeus branches leave within or proximal to the spiral groove.
points.quote: Within or proximal to the spiral groove, two motor branches are given off.

points.text: The deep branch becomes the purely motor posterior interosseous nerve; the superficial branch is sensory with an autonomous zone over the first interosseous space.
points.quote: referred to as the posterior interosseous nerve. This purely motor nerve innervates the following muscles

points.text: The femoral nerve runs between psoas and iliacus, supplying both hip flexors; its quadriceps branch serves the patellar reflex.
points.quote: The nerve runs in the groove between the psoas and iliacus muscles (flexors of the thigh, both of which it supplies)

points.text: The saphenous nerve is the longest sensory branch of the femoral nerve and runs in the adductor (Hunter) canal.
points.quote: The saphenous nerve, the longest sensory branch of the femoral nerve, descends to the knee in the subsartorial adductor (Hunter) canal

points.text: Sciatic fascicles are somatotopic: L5 fibers lie anterolaterally and S1 fibers posteromedially.
points.quote: Fascicles emerging from L5 nerve root are ordered in anterolateral positions within sciatic nerve cross sections, while fascicles emerging from S1 appear posteromedially.

points.text: The sciatic nerve divides at the popliteal apex into the tibial and common peroneal nerves.
points.quote: it divides into its two terminal branches, the tibial (medial popliteal) nerve (L4-S3) and the common peroneal

points.text: The common peroneal nerve divides within peroneus longus into the deep and the superficial peroneal nerves.
points.quote: where it divides into two branches: the deep peroneal (anterior tibial) nerve and the superficial peroneal nerve

localizationRules.rule: Thenar sensory loss puts the lesion above the wrist
localizationRules.explanation: In carpal tunnel syndrome the thenar eminence is spared because the palmar cutaneous branch leaves proximal to the wrist; sensory loss there means the median lesion is more proximal.
localizationRules.quote: Therefore, if this area shows a sensory loss, the lesion is proximal to the wrist joint.

localizationRules.rule: Radial lesion: spiral groove spares the triceps
localizationRules.explanation: A high axillary radial lesion also takes out the triceps and the triceps reflex; at the spiral groove the triceps branches have already left the nerve, so the triceps and its reflex are spared.
localizationRules.quote: The triceps muscle (and therefore the triceps reflex) is spared because the branches to the muscle have a proximal origin.

localizationRules.rule: Ulnar lesion at the wrist spares FCU and FDP III-IV
localizationRules.explanation: The wrist lesion gives the intrinsic hand findings but leaves the flexor carpi ulnaris and ulnar half of flexor digitorum profundus intact; their involvement points higher.
localizationRules.quote: except that the flexor carpi ulnaris and the flexor digitorum profundus III and IV are spared

localizationRules.rule: Where is the ulnar lesion relative to its sensory branches
localizationRules.explanation: A lesion distal to the palmar and dorsal cutaneous branches leaves the proximal palm and dorsum of the hand spared and the loss is confined to the distal palm and fifth finger palmar surface.
localizationRules.quote: If the lesion is distal to these two branches, the sensory loss is restricted to the distal palm and the palmar surfaces of the fifth finger

localizationRules.rule: Femoral lesion at the inguinal ligament spares hip flexion
localizationRules.explanation: Branches to iliacus and psoas arise proximally, so a lesion at the inguinal ligament leaves thigh flexion intact, while a more proximal lesion (lumbar plexus or pelvis) weakens it.
localizationRules.quote: Lesions at the inguinal ligament result in similar findings, but thigh flexion is spared because of the more proximal origin of the femoral nerve

localizationRules.rule: Sciatic lesions hit the peroneal division more
localizationRules.explanation: Sciatic injury more often affects the lateral (peroneal) division than the medial (tibial) division, so a foot drop does not prove a peroneal nerve lesion.
localizationRules.quote: In general, sciatic lesions tend to affect the peroneal division more than the tibial division in about 75% of cases

keySyndromes.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Nocturnal wrist and hand pain or paresthesias + paresis and atrophy of abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis + sensory loss on the radial palm and first three-and-a-half fingers
keySyndromes.clue: The lumbricals are often normal and the thenar eminence skin is spared; Tinel, Phalen and flick signs support the diagnosis.
keySyndromes.quote: Paresis and atrophy of the APB and opponens pollicis muscles are present.

keySyndromes.name: Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome (Kiloh-Nevin)
keySyndromes.triad: Forearm pain + weak flexion of the terminal phalanges of the thumb and second and third fingers + pinch attitude + normal sensation
keySyndromes.clue: A purely motor syndrome from the anterior interosseous branch; mild pronation weakness comes from pronator quadratus.
keySyndromes.quote: There is a characteristic pinch attitude of the hand while attempting to make a full circle by applying the pulp of the thumb

keySyndromes.name: Ulnar neuropathy (claw hand and Froment sign)
keySyndromes.triad: Atrophy of hypothenar eminence and interossei + claw-hand deformity + Froment sign + sensory loss on the fifth and ulnar half of the fourth finger and ulnar hand
keySyndromes.clue: Froment sign reflects adductor pollicis weakness; all three sensory branches are affected with lesions at or above the elbow.
keySyndromes.quote: As a result of adductor pollicis affection, Froment prehensile thumb sign (signe du journal) may be present

keySyndromes.name: Cubital tunnel syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Paresthesias and sensory loss in the ulnar fourth and fifth digits + weakness and atrophy of ulnar-innervated hand muscles + ulnar flexion maneuver aggravating symptoms
keySyndromes.clue: The syndrome matches an ulnar lesion above the elbow, but the flexor carpi ulnaris is often spared.
keySyndromes.quote: Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow often spares the flexor carpi ulnaris muscle.

keySyndromes.name: Radial neuropathy at the spiral groove (Saturday night palsy)
keySyndromes.triad: Wrist drop + weak extension of wrist and metacarpophalangeal joints + preserved triceps and triceps reflex
keySyndromes.clue: Typical after a deep or alcohol-deepened sleep; sensation on the extensor arm is spared, forearm sensation may or may not be.
keySyndromes.quote: The most common presentation of acute retrohumeral compression is one in which the subject wakens, often from a deep sleep

keySyndromes.name: Posterior interosseous nerve syndrome
keySyndromes.triad: Radial deviation of the wrist on making a fist + drop-finger deformity at all five metacarpophalangeal joints + weak thumb extension and abduction
keySyndromes.clue: The supinator and the superficial radial sensory branch are often spared; the extensor carpi radialis is unaffected.
keySyndromes.quote: Because the extensor carpi radialis is unaffected while the extensor carpi ulnaris is paretic, the wrist deviates radially

keySyndromes.name: Common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head
keySyndromes.triad: Weak toe and foot dorsiflexion + weak foot eversion + variable sensory loss on the dorsum of the foot and lateral distal lower leg
keySyndromes.clue: The deep branch is more often affected than the whole nerve; weakness is usually greater in deep peroneal muscles.
keySyndromes.quote: When both branches (deep and superficial) are affected, there is paresis or paralysis of toe and foot dorsiflexion and of foot eversion.

keySyndromes.name: Meralgia paresthetica (lateral femoral cutaneous neuropathy)
keySyndromes.triad: Pain and paresthesias in an oval area of the lateral or anterolateral thigh + sensory loss in the lateral femoral cutaneous distribution + no motor deficit (purely sensory nerve)
keySyndromes.clue: Compression at the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine, especially in obese people wearing constricting garments.
keySyndromes.quote: These paresthesias are associated with sensory loss in the cutaneous distribution of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve

boardTraps.text: A partial sciatic lesion can involve only the peroneal or only the tibial trunk and be mistaken for a common peroneal or tibial neuropathy.
boardTraps.quote: partial sciatic lesions may differentially involve these trunks and thereby cause misleading localization deficits.

boardTraps.text: A Martin-Gruber median-to-ulnar anastomosis can spare hand muscles in a proximal ulnar lesion.
boardTraps.quote: if a patient has an ulnar neuropathy above the forearm, these muscles may be spared or minimally involved if a median-ulnar communication is present

boardTraps.text: In radial palsy, finger abduction can look weak because the wrist is not fixed, which can be mistaken for an ulnar problem.
boardTraps.quote: finger abduction by the dorsal interossei may seem weak when a radial nerve palsy prevents fixation of the wrist

boardTraps.text: Isolated hand weakness in an ulnar pattern can be cerebral rather than peripheral (pseudoulnar palsy, with contralateral carotid stenosis in the reported patients).
boardTraps.quote: Pseudoulnar nerve palsy refers to isolated hand weakness apparently in an ulnar distribution that is due to contralateral cerebral infarction

boardTraps.text: Ankle plantar flexor weakness greater than dorsiflexor weakness argues against polyneuropathy and for a conus-cauda or other intraspinal cause.
boardTraps.quote: intraspinal disease (e.g., conus-cauda equina tumor, spinal muscular atrophy, spinal stenosis, and carcinomatous meningitis) rather than peripheral polyneuropathy should be suspected

boardTraps.text: ALS (an anterior horn cell disease, not a nerve disease) gives dissociated atrophy of intrinsic hand muscles (split hand) that innervation alone does not explain.
boardTraps.quote: the thenar muscles, the APB, and the FDI muscle are predominantly affected, with relative preservation of the hypothenar muscle
